Bombus californicus browsing on a sage blossom for nectar. Note her extended tongue and lack of pollen on her hind legs. Note also that this species of bumble bee has no yellow hairs on their faces nor the top of the head, unlike the other common bumble bees in this area. The plant looks like black sage, Salvia mellifera, but it could be another species, cultivar or hybrid. There are two photos of the same bee in this upload.

California Bumble Bee with impressive corbiculae. Wikipedia quotes on Pollen Basket, “Either honey or nectar is used to moisten the dry pollen, producing the product known as bee pollen or bee bread. The mixing of the pollen with nectar or honey changes the color of the pollen. The color of the pollen can help identify the pollen source.” This bee was feeding on the last few flowers of Wild Radish.

California Bumblebee (Bombus californicus), photographed along the Stevens Creek Trail in Mountain View, CA. I was surprised to see this bumblebee appear amongst the small cloud of Yellow-faced Bumblebees (Bombus vosnesenskii) who were working the Wild Radish (Raphanus sativus) along the Stevens Creek Trail. Interestingly, this one had no yellow on its face, which made me think immediately of the Californica Bumblebee. I also noticed that it was significantly larger than the many Yellow-faced Bumblees. That said, I don't have much experience in the field with B. californicus, so this identification could be wrong.

Four individuals have been regularly returning to the same clump of grass to sleep each evening after foraging amongst the wildflowers in my yard. The yard is covered in native grasses but they always return to the exact spot, and three of them always sleep very close together on the same grass stalk while the fourth one chooses to sleep about 12" away, almost as if it's the designated sentry. Absolutely fascinating. If anyone can explain their behavior I'd love to learn more about this bumblebee species! (Update: one month later, one bee is still returning each evening to sleep in the same spot)

This area is dominated by non-native grasses, with Avena sp. being the most conspicuous, but Bromus madritensis subsp. rubens and B. diandrus are also present. Patches of native shrubs and forbs are dotted throughout the area, including Malosma laurina, Acmispon glaber, Asclepias fascicularis, and Asclepias eriocarpa. I observed this Crotch's Bumble Bee feeding on White Sage (Salvia apiana) flowers. "Bombus crotchii inhabits open grassland and scrub habitats. Nesting occurs underground. Males perch and chase moving objects in search of mates. This species is classified as a short-tongued species, whose food plants include Asclepias, Chaenactis, Lupinus, Medicago, Phacelia, and Salvia (Williams et al. 2014). Bumble bees are social insects that live in colonies composed of a queen, workers, and reproductives (males and new queens). Colonies are annual and only the new, mated queens overwinter. These queens emerge from hibernation in the early spring and immediately start foraging for pollen and nectar and begin to search for a nest site. Nests are often located underground in abandoned rodent nests, or above ground in tufts of grass, old bird nests, rock piles, or cavities in dead trees. Initially, the queen does all of the foraging and care for the colony until the first workers emerge and assist with these duties. Bumble bees collect both nectar and pollen of the plants that they pollinate. In general, bumble bees forage from a diversity of plants, although individual species can vary greatly in their plant preferences, largely due to differences in tongue length. Bumble bees are well-known to engage in buzz pollination, a very effective foraging technique in which they sonicate the flowers to vibrate the pollen loose from the anthers. Tomatoes (Solanaceae), blueberries (Ericaceae), and many other important food plants are pollinated by bumble bees in this way."(Endangered Species Coalition)

Conservation Status: Endangered (EN) (IUCN Red List). Genus Bombus (Bumblebees) are our only native social bees. They are warm blooded allowing them to fly at cooler temperatures than most pollinators. Kaufman Field Guide to Insects of North America, Eaton and Kaufman, 2006, p. 344-345. BugGuide: https://bugguide.net/index.php?q=search&keys=bombus+crotchii xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx How to identify if it’s a Male or Female Bumble Bee: Male has no stinger so it can be handled if necessary. “Generally, male bumblebees have hairy hind legs without a pollen basket (though beware female cuckoo bees, which also have hairy hind legs). Males also usually have more facial hair than females (either queens or workers) – and in several species this is a bright, obvious yellow. Males also generally have longer, more straggly hair, so if your bee has hairy legs, a moustache, and looks slightly unkempt it’s probably a male. Behavior can be a useful tool to separate males from workers and queens: because males do not have to collect pollen for the nest, they tend to sit lazily on flowers. They may also be observed flying along hedgerows searching for a mate. They do not feed during this time, so will land briefly on a surface, and then fly off again. They often patrol the same area for a while, so you may see the same bee repeating the circuit over and over again. In contrast, females tend to be much busier, flying quickly from flower to flower, and rarely wasting time by resting on flowers. The time of year can also be helpful – males become common in late summer and autumn, whereas females are present throughout the whole lifecycle." Bumble Bee I.D. Tips: https://www.bumblebeeconservation.org/identification-tips/ xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx "There are 6 taxonomic families of Bees: Apidae; (ap-ih-dee) These are the really common, really big bees. Included in this family are the European honeybees, BUMBLE BEES and carpenter bees. Andrenidae; (an-dren-ih-dee) These bees tend towards being small and hairy. They make their homes in the ground so are often called mining bees, or sand bees. Generally, they are so small they can fit in tiny flowers, like the bell-shaped blossoms that hang from Manzanita (Arctostaphylos). Colletidae; (co-lect-ih-dee) Included in this family are two genera (Colletes and Hylaeus) that are identifiable by their unique faces. If you are lucky enough to study the face of a landed Colletes, you can identify it by its distinctly triangular face. Hylaeus usually has a black body that is contrasted to the yellow markings on its face that make it look like it’s wearing a mask. Halictidae; (ha-lect-ih-dee) These bees are commonly called sweat bees because apparently, they like to land on human skin and drink sweat, although I’ve never observed this. I like to call them jewel bees because they often are metallic in sheen and bright in color. Megachilidae; (mega-chill-ih-dee) These bees include the mason or the wool-carder bees. They make their homes inside hollowed out twigs or in tunnels made by other insects like beetles. The invasive and common Anthidium manicatum is a regular visitor to the Santa Cruz mountains. Melittidae; (mel-it-tih-dee) The most-rare of the bee family types in California. Feeding exclusively on Clarkia flowers in the California chaparral, Hesperapis regularis is one of a small number of native species" Native Bees: Get to Know Native Bees of the Santa Cruz Mountains (California) with Obi Kaufmann. https://openspacetrust.org/blog/native-bees/

Two Crotch's Bumble Bees (Bombus crotchii) were observed on Black Sage (Salvia mellifera) at the Claremont Colleges Bernard Field Station (BFS). These bees were conspicuously large, so I think they were queens, which would be consistent with the March sighting date. The Black Sage plants these bees were on are part of the plantings around the Robert Redford Conservancy for Southern California Sustainability. The plantings are all of native plants that occur on the BFS, and they were propagated by California Botanic Garden from indigenous plants on the site. The other individual (https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/56541202) had something on the back of its thorax that I think are pollinia. I am not sure what the source of these might be. Nothing blooming at the BFS at the time had pollinia. It's possible some of the neighboring houses had orchids in bloom. At least one of the neighbors has grown orchids in the past.

This area is dominated by non-native grasses, with Avena sp. being the most conspicuous, but Bromus madritensis subsp. rubens and B. diandrus are also present. I observed this Crotch's Bumble Bee feeding on White Sage (Salvia apiana) flowers. "Bombus crotchii inhabits open grassland and scrub habitats. Nesting occurs underground. Males perch and chase moving objects in search of mates. This species is classified as a short-tongued species, whose food plants include Asclepias, Chaenactis, Lupinus, Medicago, Phacelia, and Salvia (Williams et al. 2014). Bumble bees are social insects that live in colonies composed of a queen, workers, and reproductives (males and new queens). Colonies are annual and only the new, mated queens overwinter. These queens emerge from hibernation in the early spring and immediately start foraging for pollen and nectar and begin to search for a nest site. Nests are often located underground in abandoned rodent nests, or above ground in tufts of grass, old bird nests, rock piles, or cavities in dead trees. Initially, the queen does all of the foraging and care for the colony until the first workers emerge and assist with these duties. Bumble bees collect both nectar and pollen of the plants that they pollinate. In general, bumble bees forage from a diversity of plants, although individual species can vary greatly in their plant preferences, largely due to differences in tongue length. Bumble bees are well-known to engage in buzz pollination, a very effective foraging technique in which they sonicate the flowers to vibrate the pollen loose from the anthers. Tomatoes (Solanaceae), blueberries (Ericaceae), and many other important food plants are pollinated by bumble bees in this way."(Endangered Species Coalition)

Conservation Status: Endangered (EN) (IUCN Red List). Genus Bombus (Bumblebees) are our only native social bees. They are warm blooded allowing them to fly at cooler temperatures than most pollinators. Kaufman Field Guide to Insects of North America, Eaton and Kaufman, 2006, p. 344-345. BugGuide: https://bugguide.net/index.php?q=search&keys=bombus+crotchii xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx How to identify if it’s a Male or Female Bumble Bee: Male has no stinger so it can be handled if necessary. “Generally, male bumblebees have hairy hind legs without a pollen basket (though beware female cuckoo bees, which also have hairy hind legs). Males also usually have more facial hair than females (either queens or workers) – and in several species this is a bright, obvious yellow. Males also generally have longer, more straggly hair, so if your bee has hairy legs, a moustache, and looks slightly unkempt it’s probably a male. Behavior can be a useful tool to separate males from workers and queens: because males do not have to collect pollen for the nest, they tend to sit lazily on flowers. They may also be observed flying along hedgerows searching for a mate. They do not feed during this time, so will land briefly on a surface, and then fly off again. They often patrol the same area for a while, so you may see the same bee repeating the circuit over and over again. In contrast, females tend to be much busier, flying quickly from flower to flower, and rarely wasting time by resting on flowers. The time of year can also be helpful – males become common in late summer and autumn, whereas females are present throughout the whole lifecycle." Bumble Bee I.D. Tips: https://www.bumblebeeconservation.org/identification-tips/ xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx "There are 6 taxonomic families of Bees: Apidae; (ap-ih-dee) These are the really common, really big bees. Included in this family are the European honeybees, BUMBLE BEES and carpenter bees. Andrenidae; (an-dren-ih-dee) These bees tend towards being small and hairy. They make their homes in the ground so are often called mining bees, or sand bees. Generally, they are so small they can fit in tiny flowers, like the bell-shaped blossoms that hang from Manzanita (Arctostaphylos). Colletidae; (co-lect-ih-dee) Included in this family are two genera (Colletes and Hylaeus) that are identifiable by their unique faces. If you are lucky enough to study the face of a landed Colletes, you can identify it by its distinctly triangular face. Hylaeus usually has a black body that is contrasted to the yellow markings on its face that make it look like it’s wearing a mask. Halictidae; (ha-lect-ih-dee) These bees are commonly called sweat bees because apparently, they like to land on human skin and drink sweat, although I’ve never observed this. I like to call them jewel bees because they often are metallic in sheen and bright in color. Megachilidae; (mega-chill-ih-dee) These bees include the mason or the wool-carder bees. They make their homes inside hollowed out twigs or in tunnels made by other insects like beetles. The invasive and common Anthidium manicatum is a regular visitor to the Santa Cruz mountains. Melittidae; (mel-it-tih-dee) The most-rare of the bee family types in California. Feeding exclusively on Clarkia flowers in the California chaparral, Hesperapis regularis is one of a small number of native species" Native Bees: Get to Know Native Bees of the Santa Cruz Mountains (California) with Obi Kaufmann. https://openspacetrust.org/blog/native-bees/

Two Crotch's Bumble Bees (Bombus crotchii) were observed on Black Sage (Salvia mellifera) at the Claremont Colleges Bernard Field Station (BFS). These bees were conspicuously large, so I think they were queens, which would be consistent with the March sighting date. The Black Sage plants these bees were on are part of the plantings around the Robert Redford Conservancy for Southern California Sustainability. The plantings are all of native plants that occur on the BFS, and they were propagated by California Botanic Garden from indigenous plants on the site. The other individual (https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/56541202) had something on the back of its thorax that I think are pollinia. I am not sure what the source of these might be. Nothing blooming at the BFS at the time had pollinia. It's possible some of the neighboring houses had orchids in bloom. At least one of the neighbors has grown orchids in the past.

Here are Bombus (genus) key traits: • Body structure: They have a large, rounded body divided into head, thorax, and abdomen, typically 1.5–2.5 cm long. Colonies are smaller than honey bee hives, often under 200 individuals. • Pollination tools: Workers have corbiculae (pollen baskets) on their hind legs and are capable of buzz pollination—vibrating flowers to release pollen, especially useful for crops like tomatoes. • Flight and foraging: They’re strong fliers, active in cooler, cloudier conditions than many other bees. How to identify if it’s a MALE or FEMALE Bumble Bee: by INat makarii_loskutov who handles many: Male has no stinger so it can be handled if necessary. “Generally, male bumblebees have hairy hind legs without a pollen basket (though beware female cuckoo bees, which also have hairy hind legs). Males also usually have more facial hair than females (either queens or workers) – and in several species this is a bright, obvious yellow. Males also generally have longer, more straggly hair, so if your bee has hairy legs, a moustache, and looks slightly unkempt it’s probably a male. Behavior can be a useful tool to separate males from workers and queens: because males do not have to collect pollen for the nest, they tend to sit lazily on flowers. They may also be observed flying along hedgerows searching for a mate. They do not feed during this time, so will land briefly on a surface, and then fly off again. INat susanna_h Hymenoptera (ants, bees, wasps, sawflies) are characterized by two pairs of membranous wings joined by tiny hooks (hamuli), chewing or chewing-sucking mouthparts, complete metamorphosis, and mandibulate mouthparts. Hymenoptera are predators. Hymenoptera order is split into sawflies (broad waist) and wasps/bees/ants (narrow waist). Key Characteristics of Hymenoptera: • Diversity: Over 150,000 described species worldwide, including ants, bees, wasps, and sawflies. • Wings: Typically two pairs of membranous wings; forewings larger than hindwings. The wings are coupled by hamuli (small hooks). Some castes (e.g., worker ants) are wingless. • Body Form:• In Symphyta (sawflies, horntails): broad connection between thorax and abdomen. • In Apocrita (ants, bees, wasps): narrow “wasp waist” between thorax and abdomen. • Mouthparts: Primarily mandibulate (chewing); in bees, modified into a chewing-lapping apparatus for nectar. • Metamorphosis: Holometabolous (complete metamorphosis: egg → larva → pupa → adult). • Feeding:• Sawfly larvae are herbivorous. • Many wasps are predatory or parasitoid, laying eggs in or on other insects. • Bees are nectar and pollen feeders, crucial pollinators. • Ants are omnivorous, with diverse diets. • Sociality: Includes some of the most advanced eusocial insects (ants, honeybees, some wasps), with division of labor, cooperative brood care, and overlapping generations. Most species, however, are solitary. • Ecological Role:• Pollinators (bees, some wasps). • Biological control agents (parasitoid wasps regulating pest populations). • Soil engineers and ecosystem influencers (ants). I believe these photos are all of the same individual bee. This bee was about 2 cm long. I noticed about 7 other bees with similar size, but without the middle yellow stripe, so they were probably a different type of bumble bee. They seemed hyper energized and would make vigorous buzzing as they flew around me and the shrubs. Their mood seemed more intense than I am used to seeing bumble bees and circled me several times with loud buzzing even though I was standing very still and was not interacting with them. However, they did not seem threatening towards me. They would occasionally land on these bushes (manzanita?) and carefully poke their proboscis into the tiny 7mm long pink bell shaped flowers. I wonder if these are newly born/emerged bumble bees. They seemed to have so much energy.

I found this bee situated on the top of a cluster of flowers protruding from a flowerbed. It was most likely in this area because the flowers provide bees with pollen and nectar. Collecting these components are vital in order for this insect to feed and thrive. This is because nectar provides energy and pollen provides essential nutrients, such as proteins. I caught this organism with a net and put it in a jar to observe. This organism was large and fuzzy with numerous branched hairs that covered its body. It was also striped with the colors black and yellow. The first segment of the hind tarsi on the insect was enlarged and bore a pollen basket. While I was observing, the insect flew frantically around the inside the jar the entire time. It emitted a distinctly loud buzzing noise. I found a couple of these organisms across the top of the flower clusters. The insect above was collected and pinned in a safe manner.

I found this bumblebee clinging to a leaf- that seemed an odd place to sleep. As I moved in closer to investigate, and to confirm the bee was still alive, I accidentally knocked it from its perch. It was alive and able to walk, but apparentally unable to fly. I moved it to a nearby forget-me-not flower in case it needed nectar, and watched it feed on the flower and crawl from blossom to blossom, however it was still apparently unable to fly away. I wonder if it was sick or had a parasite, or if it was nearing the end of its natural lifespan.

Here are Bombus (genus) key traits: • Body structure: They have a large, rounded body divided into head, thorax, and abdomen, typically 1.5–2.5 cm long. Their dense hair (setae) helps trap pollen. • Coloration: Most species show black with yellow, orange, or white banding. Mimicry among species can make visual ID tricky. • Social behavior: They form seasonal colonies led by a single queen. Colonies are smaller than honey bee hives, often under 200 individuals. • Pollination tools: Workers have corbiculae (pollen baskets) on their hind legs and are capable of buzz pollination—vibrating flowers to release pollen, especially useful for crops like tomatoes. • Flight and foraging: They’re strong fliers, active in cooler, cloudier conditions than many other bees. In contrast, females tend to be much busier, flying quickly from flower to flower, and rarely wasting time by resting on flowers. INat susanna_h Hymenoptera (ants, bees, wasps, sawflies) are characterized by two pairs of membranous wings joined by tiny hooks (hamuli), chewing or chewing-sucking mouthparts, complete metamorphosis, and mandibulate mouthparts. Hymenoptera are predators. Hymenoptera order is split into sawflies (broad waist) and wasps/bees/ants (narrow waist). Key Characteristics of Hymenoptera: • Diversity: Over 150,000 described species worldwide, including ants, bees, wasps, and sawflies. • Wings: Typically two pairs of membranous wings; forewings larger than hindwings. The wings are coupled by hamuli (small hooks). Some castes (e.g., worker ants) are wingless. • Body Form:• In Symphyta (sawflies, horntails): broad connection between thorax and abdomen. • In Apocrita (ants, bees, wasps): narrow “wasp waist” between thorax and abdomen. • Mouthparts: Primarily mandibulate (chewing); in bees, modified into a chewing-lapping apparatus for nectar. • Metamorphosis: Holometabolous (complete metamorphosis: egg → larva → pupa → adult). • Feeding:• Sawfly larvae are herbivorous. • Many wasps are predatory or parasitoid, laying eggs in or on other insects. • Bees are nectar and pollen feeders, crucial pollinators. • Ants are omnivorous, with diverse diets. • Sociality: Includes some of the most advanced eusocial insects (ants, honeybees, some wasps), with division of labor, cooperative brood care, and overlapping generations. Most species, however, are solitary. • Ecological Role:• Pollinators (bees, some wasps). • Biological control agents (parasitoid wasps regulating pest populations). • Soil engineers and ecosystem influencers (ants). I believe these photos are all of the same individual bee. This bee was about 2 cm long. I noticed about 7 other bees with similar size, but without the middle yellow stripe, so they were probably a different type of bumble bee. They seemed hyper energized and would make vigorous buzzing as they flew around me and the shrubs. Their mood seemed more intense than I am used to seeing bumble bees and circled me several times with loud buzzing even though I was standing very still and was not interacting with them. However, they did not seem threatening towards me. They would occasionally land on these bushes (manzanita?) and carefully poke their proboscis into the tiny 7mm long pink bell shaped flowers. I wonder if these are newly born/emerged bumble bees. They seemed to have so much energy.

I considered Bombus melanopygus or B. bifarius but lack familiarity with identified specimens. This was a rescue from a friend’s chicken coop. I found this bee situated on the top of a cluster of flowers protruding from a flowerbed. It was most likely in this area because the flowers provide bees with pollen and nectar. Collecting these components are vital in order for this insect to feed and thrive. This is because nectar provides energy and pollen provides essential nutrients, such as proteins. I caught this organism with a net and put it in a jar to observe. This organism was large and fuzzy with numerous branched hairs that covered its body. It was also striped with the colors black and yellow. The first segment of the hind tarsi on the insect was enlarged and bore a pollen basket. While I was observing, the insect flew frantically around the inside the jar the entire time. It emitted a distinctly loud buzzing noise. I found a couple of these organisms across the top of the flower clusters. The insect above was collected and pinned in a safe manner.

I found this bumblebee clinging to a leaf- that seemed an odd place to sleep. As I moved in closer to investigate, and to confirm the bee was still alive, I accidentally knocked it from its perch. It was alive and able to walk, but apparentally unable to fly. I moved it to a nearby forget-me-not flower in case it needed nectar, and watched it feed on the flower and crawl from blossom to blossom, however it was still apparently unable to fly away. I wonder if it was sick or had a parasite, or if it was nearing the end of its natural lifespan.

I thought this was a yellow faced bumble bee but she has too much yellow I think. She crashed in the yard due to bad weather and fatigue and my dog got her. Luckily she was ok but would not move so I packed her in a jar with a paper towel to snuggle in with the tiniest bit of water on one corner in case she was thirsty and she stayed a few days until the storm passed. When she woke up and was ready to leave her jar I made a bouquet for her and put down some sugar water on a cotton pad but she only wanted sugar water. She is very clever and climbed up of a rock that was warmed by the sun and flew away once she was warm enough.

This 7.7 mile loop kicked my butt, especially since I went very slow iNatting like a maniac on the way south before realizing how slow I was going... will I ever learn? Got here by riding BART from Berryessa to 19th ST Oakland before transferring to Yellow line to Concord, then took the 10 bus to Clayton and bicycled to the park entrance. About 2 hours ride each way but no gas emission and only a little slower than a drive here either way! BugGuide: https://bugguide.net/index.php?q=search&keys=Anthophora%20bomboides xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx Irene's Bumble Bees (Bombus genus) observations on INaturalist, worldwide: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?taxon_id=52775&user_id=aparrot1&verifiable=any Bumble Bees in the genus Bombus are robust, hairy bees known for their powerful flight and critical role in pollination. Here are Bombus (genus) key traits: • Body structure: They have a large, rounded body divided into head, thorax, and abdomen, typically 1.5–2.5 cm long. Their dense hair (setae) helps trap pollen. • Coloration: Most species show black with yellow, orange, or white banding. Mimicry among species can make visual ID tricky. • Social behavior: They form seasonal colonies led by a single queen. Colonies are smaller than honey bee hives, often under 200 individuals. • Pollination tools: Workers have corbiculae (pollen baskets) on their hind legs and are capable of buzz pollination—vibrating flowers to release pollen, especially useful for crops like tomatoes. • Flight and foraging: They’re strong fliers, active in cooler, cloudier conditions than many other bees. Many species are generalist foragers, while some specialize in deep flowers thanks to long tongues. • Defense: Females can sting repeatedly but are generally non-aggressive unless provoked. xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx Irene's Apine Bees (Apinae) Subfamily observations on INaturalist, worldwide: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?taxon_id=199939&user_id=aparrot1&verifiable=any BEES In General: Irene's Bees (Epifamily Anthophila) on INaturalist, worldwide: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?taxon_id=630955&user_id=aparrot1 Bees (Epifamily Anthophila): There are 1000+ species of native Bees in California. Honey Bees (introduced from Old World), Social Sweat Bees, and Bumble Bees are social. Most other bees are solitary. Bees forage on nectar and pollen--nectar as an energy source and pollen for protein and other nutrients. Most pollen is used as food for bee larvae. Predators of bees include birds such as bee-eaters, insect predators such as dragonflies, and mammals. Bee pollination is important both ecologically and commercially. Bees provide crucial ecological services that enhance ecosystem resilience, food security and support the agricultural economy. There has been a huge decline of bees worldwide in the past few decades, primarily due to human pesticide use to kill other insects, and habitat loss of native plants. A Yellow-faced Bumblebee (Bombus vosnesenskii) pollinating the flowers of some Coast Woolly Sunflower (Eriophyllum staechadifolium) at Greyhound Rock County Park. The off-white/pale yellow coloration of the hairs on its clypeus (face), anterior scutum (front part of its thorax), and fourth tergites (abdominal segment) is due to natural variation; normally, these hairs are brighter yellow in color. This was a fairly common species at this location. This set has three shots of the same individual bee, taken as it flitted from flower to flower, hunting for nectar. The second shot is probably the best shot of it, as it shows the faint off-white/pale yellow hairs that cover the bee's anterior scutum, head, and clypeus. It also shows that the rest of the bee's hairs are black, except for those on its 4th tergites, which are also the same of-white/pale yellow color. This distribution of yellow and black hairs is a distinctive field mark for this species, separating it from all of the other bumblebees of western North America.

COMPARE Fog-belt Bumble Bee (Bombus caliginosus) Yellow abdominal stripes DO continue around underside. xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx COMPARE TO Yellow-faced Bumble Bee (Bombus vosnesenskii) is in the Honey Bees, Bumble Bees, and Allies (Apidae) family. It is about 16mm long. Yellow abdominal stripe DOES NOT continue around underside in this species. "There is a very similar species, Bombus caliginosus, that has a range that overlaps with Yellow-faced Bumble Bee (B. vosnesenskii). The easiest way to tell the two apart is to look at the yellow abdominal stripe. In B. caliginosus, it continues on the underside, while in B. vosnesenskii, the underside is black." Per INat @ domingozungri. Photo comparison on BugGuide https://bugguide.net/index.php?q=search&keys=Bombus+vosnesenskii https://bugguide.net/index.php?q=search&keys=Bombus+caliginosus Link to confirmed observation of Yellow-faced Bumble Bee showing the underside: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/222367270 And a few more: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?taxon_id=57689&user_id=aparrot1&verifiable=any Genus Bombus (Bumblebees) are our only native social bees. They are warm blooded allowing them to fly at cooler temperatures than most pollinators. Native Bees https://openspacetrust.org/blog/native-bees/ Pollen Basket: The pollen basket is located on the female bee’s hind legs and consists of hairs surrounding a concave receptacle. As the bee visits a flower, she grooms herself and brushes pollen sticking to her body toward her hind legs. She then packs the pollen into the pollen basket. To help keep the pollen together during flight, some nectar is mixed in. Hairs on the pollen basket hold it all in place. Amazing! Kaufman Field Guide to Insects of North America, Eaton and Kaufman, 2006, p. 344-345. How to identify if it’s a Male or Female Bumble Bee: Male has no stinger so it can be handled if necessary. (per INat makarii_loskutov who handles many) “Generally, male bumblebees have hairy hind legs without a pollen basket (though beware female cuckoo bees, which also have hairy hind legs). Males also usually have more facial hair than females (either queens or workers) – and in several species this is a bright, obvious yellow. Males also generally have longer, more straggly hair, so if your bee has hairy legs, a moustache, and looks slightly unkempt it’s probably a male. Behavior can be a useful tool to separate males from workers and queens: because males do not have to collect pollen for the nest, they tend to sit lazily on flowers. They may also be observed flying along hedgerows searching for a mate. They do not feed during this time, so will land briefly on a surface, and then fly off again. They often patrol the same area for a while, so you may see the same bee repeating the circuit over and over again. In contrast, females tend to be much busier, flying quickly from flower to flower, and rarely wasting time by resting on flowers. The time of year can also be helpful – males become common in late summer and autumn, whereas females are present throughout the whole lifecycle." xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx Irene's Bumble Bees (Bombus genus) on INaturalist, worldwide: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?taxon_id=52775&user_id=aparrot1&verifiable=any Irene's Bees (Epifamily Anthophila) on INaturalist, worldwide: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?taxon_id=630955&user_id=aparrot1 Bees (Epifamily Anthophila) "Bees forage on nectar and pollen--nectar as an energy source and pollen for protein and other nutrients. Most pollen is used as food for bee larvae. Predators of bees include birds such as bee-eaters, insect predators such as dragonflies, and mammals. Bee pollination is important both ecologically and commercially. Bees provide crucial ecological services that enhance ecosystem resilience, food security and support the agricultural economy. There has been a huge decline of bees worldwide in the past few decades, primarily due to human pesticide use to kill other insects, and habitat loss of native plants. "There are 6 Taxonomic Families of Bees (Epifamily Anthophila): https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/630955-Anthophila: Miner, Fairy, Allied Panurgine, and Oxaeine Bees (Family Andrenidae) Honey Bees, Bumble Bees, and Allies (Family Apidae) Plasterer Bees (Family Colletidae) Sweat Bees (Family Halictidae) Mason, Leafcutter, Carder, and Resin Bees (Family Megachilidae) Melittid Bees (Family Melittidae) Swift and Comb-bearer Bees (Family Stenotritidae) Beekeeping Beyond the Hive: The Surprising Secrets of Bees Native • Wild • Managed "Bees are the wispy sprites that connect the plant kingdom to the animal kingdom; they are the ties that bind the natural world together. Because of bees, flowering plants grace our planet with beauty and food." (INaturalist) rustybee's website: https://www.honeybeesuite.com/ Field Guide to California Insects, by Kip Will, J. Gross, D. Powell, 2nd ed., 2020 BugGuide: Arthropods: Photos of Insects, Spiders & Their Kin (US & Canada): https://bugguide.net/node/view/3/bgpage Native Bees: Get to Know Native Bees of the Santa Cruz Mountains (California) with Obi Kaufmann: https://openspacetrust.org/blog/native-bees/ Apidae; (ap-ih-dee) These are the really common, really big bees. Included in this family are the European honeybees, Bumble Bees and Carpenter Bees. Andrenidae; (an-dren-ih-dee) These bees tend towards being small and hairy. They make their homes in the ground so are often called mining bees, or sand bees. Generally, they are so small they can fit in tiny flowers, like the bell-shaped blossoms that hang from Manzanita (Arctostaphylos). Colletidae; (co-lect-ih-dee) Included in this family are two genera (Colletes and Hylaeus) that are identifiable by their unique faces. If you are lucky enough to study the face of a landed Colletes, you can identify it by its distinctly triangular face. Hylaeus usually has a black body that is contrasted to the yellow markings on its face that make it look like it’s wearing a mask. Halictidae; (ha-lect-ih-dee) These bees are commonly called sweat bees because apparently, they like to land on human skin and drink sweat, although I’ve never observed this. I like to call them jewel bees because they often are metallic in sheen and bright in color. Megachilidae; (mega-chill-ih-dee) These bees include the mason or the wool-carder bees. They make their homes inside hollowed out twigs or in tunnels made by other insects like beetles. The invasive and common Anthidium manicatum is a regular visitor to the Santa Cruz mountains. Melittidae; (mel-it-tih-dee) The most-rare of the bee family types in California. Feeding exclusively on Clarkia flowers in the California chaparral, Hesperapis regularis is one of a small number of native species" Native Bees: Get to Know Native Bees of the Santa Cruz Mountains with Obi Kaufmann. I spotted this Yellow-faced Bumblebee (Bombus vosensenskii) working a large patch of Rose Clover (Trifolium hirtum) at Russian Ridge Open Space Preserve, and I found myself following it and attempting to take its picture. The shots that came out reasonably well remind me of "Where's Waldo" pictures, with the bee playing the part of Waldo. The best of these shots is the lead photo. Here, the Yellow-faced Bumblebee came close enough for me to take a reasonably decent close-up photo of it, one that fortuitously shows the diagnostic yellow patch on its face. The California Bumblebee (Bombus californicus) is very similar in size and appearance, but lacks this yellow facial patch. The lead photo also shows the yellow band on its thorax, its eyes (one on either side of the yellow face patch), its antenna (emerging from the yellow face patch), and - if you look carefully - a bit of its tongue, which it is inserting into the corolla tube of an individual clover flower for a sip of nectar. Also visible are its two front legs. In the remaining two shots,the bee is partly to mostly obscured by the clover. In Shot 2, you can see the side of the bee's head, which again shows part of the yellow facial patch extending over the crown and just touching the yellow band on its thorax. In Shot 3, the bee is facing away from the camera, so you can easily see its abdomen and semi-translucent wings. Photographed near the main (Alpine Road) trailhead to the Rodge Trail at Russian Ridge Open Space Preserve in San Mateo County, CA.

Link to Coyote Mint (Monardella villosa) host plant observation https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/119579575 Yellow-faced Bumble Bee (Bombus vosnesenskii) Approx length, 16mm. Yellow abdominal stripe DOES NOT continue around underside in this species. "There is a very similar species, Bombus caliginosus, that has a range that overlaps with Yellow-faced Bumble Bee (B. vosnesenskii). The easiest way to tell the two apart is to look at the yellow abdominal stripe. In B. caliginosus, it continues on the underside, while in B. vosnesenskii, the underside is black." Per INat @ domingozungri. Photo comparison on BugGuide https://bugguide.net/index.php?q=search&keys=Bombus+vosnesenskii https://bugguide.net/index.php?q=search&keys=Bombus+caliginosus Link to confirmed observation of Yellow-faced Bumble Bee showing the underside: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/222367270 Genus Bombus (Bumblebees) are our only native social bees. They are warm blooded allowing them to fly at cooler temperatures than most pollinators. Native Bees https://openspacetrust.org/blog/native-bees/ Pollen Basket: The pollen basket is located on the female bee’s hind legs and consists of hairs surrounding a concave receptacle. As the bee visits a flower, she grooms herself and brushes pollen sticking to her body toward her hind legs. She then packs the pollen into the pollen basket. To help keep the pollen together during flight, some nectar is mixed in. Hairs on the pollen basket hold it all in place. Amazing! Kaufman Field Guide to Insects of North America, Eaton and Kaufman, 2006, p. 344-345. How to identify if it’s a Male or Female Bumble Bee: Male has no stinger so it can be handled if necessary. (per INat makarii_loskutov who handles many) “Generally, male bumblebees have hairy hind legs without a pollen basket (though beware female cuckoo bees, which also have hairy hind legs). Males also usually have more facial hair than females (either queens or workers) – and in several species this is a bright, obvious yellow. Males also generally have longer, more straggly hair, so if your bee has hairy legs, a moustache, and looks slightly unkempt it’s probably a male. Behavior can be a useful tool to separate males from workers and queens: because males do not have to collect pollen for the nest, they tend to sit lazily on flowers. They may also be observed flying along hedgerows searching for a mate. They do not feed during this time, so will land briefly on a surface, and then fly off again. They often patrol the same area for a while, so you may see the same bee repeating the circuit over and over again. In contrast, females tend to be much busier, flying quickly from flower to flower, and rarely wasting time by resting on flowers. The time of year can also be helpful – males become common in late summer and autumn, whereas females are present throughout the whole lifecycle." Bumble Bee I.D. Tips: https://www.bumblebeeconservation.org/identification-tips/ xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx "There are 6 taxonomic families of Bees: Apidae; (ap-ih-dee) These are the really common, really big bees. Included in this family are the European honeybees, BUMBLE BEES and carpenter bees. Andrenidae; (an-dren-ih-dee) These bees tend towards being small and hairy. They make their homes in the ground so are often called mining bees, or sand bees. Generally, they are so small they can fit in tiny flowers, like the bell-shaped blossoms that hang from Manzanita (Arctostaphylos). Colletidae; (co-lect-ih-dee) Included in this family are two genera (Colletes and Hylaeus) that are identifiable by their unique faces. If you are lucky enough to study the face of a landed Colletes, you can identify it by its distinctly triangular face. Hylaeus usually has a black body that is contrasted to the yellow markings on its face that make it look like it’s wearing a mask. Halictidae; (ha-lect-ih-dee) These bees are commonly called sweat bees because apparently, they like to land on human skin and drink sweat, although I’ve never observed this. I like to call them jewel bees because they often are metallic in sheen and bright in color. Megachilidae; (mega-chill-ih-dee) These bees include the mason or the wool-carder bees. They make their homes inside hollowed out twigs or in tunnels made by other insects like beetles. The invasive and common Anthidium manicatum is a regular visitor to the Santa Cruz mountains. Melittidae; (mel-it-tih-dee) The most-rare of the bee family types in California. Feeding exclusively on Clarkia flowers in the California chaparral, Hesperapis regularis is one of a small number of native species" Native Bees: Get to Know Native Bees of the Santa Cruz Mountains (California) with Obi Kaufmann. https://openspacetrust.org/blog/native-bees/

Underside of abdomen appears to be black. Yellow-faced Bumble Bee (Bombus vosnesenskii) Approx length, 16mm. Yellow abdominal stripe DOES NOT continue around underside in this species. "There is a very similar species, Bombus caliginosus, that has a range that overlaps with Yellow-faced Bumble Bee (B. vosnesenskii). The easiest way to tell the two apart is to look at the yellow abdominal stripe. In B. caliginosus, it continues on the underside, while in B. vosnesenskii, the underside is black." Per INat @ domingozungri. Photo comparison on BugGuide https://bugguide.net/index.php?q=search&keys=Bombus+vosnesenskii https://bugguide.net/index.php?q=search&keys=Bombus+caliginosus Link to confirmed observation of Yellow-faced Bumble Bee showing the underside: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/222367270 Genus Bombus (Bumblebees) are our only native social bees. They are warm blooded allowing them to fly at cooler temperatures than most pollinators. Native Bees https://openspacetrust.org/blog/native-bees/ Pollen Basket: The pollen basket is located on the female bee’s hind legs and consists of hairs surrounding a concave receptacle. As the bee visits a flower, she grooms herself and brushes pollen sticking to her body toward her hind legs. She then packs the pollen into the pollen basket. To help keep the pollen together during flight, some nectar is mixed in. Hairs on the pollen basket hold it all in place. Amazing! Kaufman Field Guide to Insects of North America, Eaton and Kaufman, 2006, p. 344-345. How to identify if it’s a Male or Female Bumble Bee: Male has no stinger so it can be handled if necessary. (per INat makarii_loskutov who handles many) “Generally, male bumblebees have hairy hind legs without a pollen basket (though beware female cuckoo bees, which also have hairy hind legs). Males also usually have more facial hair than females (either queens or workers) – and in several species this is a bright, obvious yellow. Males also generally have longer, more straggly hair, so if your bee has hairy legs, a moustache, and looks slightly unkempt it’s probably a male. Behavior can be a useful tool to separate males from workers and queens: because males do not have to collect pollen for the nest, they tend to sit lazily on flowers. They may also be observed flying along hedgerows searching for a mate. They do not feed during this time, so will land briefly on a surface, and then fly off again. They often patrol the same area for a while, so you may see the same bee repeating the circuit over and over again. In contrast, females tend to be much busier, flying quickly from flower to flower, and rarely wasting time by resting on flowers. The time of year can also be helpful – males become common in late summer and autumn, whereas females are present throughout the whole lifecycle." Bumble Bee I.D. Tips: https://www.bumblebeeconservation.org/identification-tips/ xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx "There are 6 taxonomic families of Bees: Apidae; (ap-ih-dee) These are the really common, really big bees. Included in this family are the European honeybees, BUMBLE BEES and carpenter bees. Andrenidae; (an-dren-ih-dee) These bees tend towards being small and hairy. They make their homes in the ground so are often called mining bees, or sand bees. Generally, they are so small they can fit in tiny flowers, like the bell-shaped blossoms that hang from Manzanita (Arctostaphylos). Colletidae; (co-lect-ih-dee) Included in this family are two genera (Colletes and Hylaeus) that are identifiable by their unique faces. If you are lucky enough to study the face of a landed Colletes, you can identify it by its distinctly triangular face. Hylaeus usually has a black body that is contrasted to the yellow markings on its face that make it look like it’s wearing a mask. Halictidae; (ha-lect-ih-dee) These bees are commonly called sweat bees because apparently, they like to land on human skin and drink sweat, although I’ve never observed this. I like to call them jewel bees because they often are metallic in sheen and bright in color. Megachilidae; (mega-chill-ih-dee) These bees include the mason or the wool-carder bees. The simplest difference is that males do not have a stinger, so they cannot sting. Their hind legs are also a good clue: males have hairy hind legs without a pollen basket, while females (workers and queens) have a smooth, shiny area on the hind leg used for carrying pollen. One caution is that female cuckoo bumble bees also lack pollen baskets, so leg hair alone is not always enough. Males usually have more facial hair than females, and in some species this hair is bright yellow and easy to see. Their overall hair tends to be longer and messier, giving them a slightly unkempt look compared with the neater appearance of workers and queens. Behavior also helps. Because males do not collect pollen for a nest, they often sit on flowers for long periods or rest between short flights. They may patrol along hedges, forest edges, or trails while searching for females, flying a repeated route and landing briefly before taking off again. Females behave differently: they move quickly from flower to flower, gather pollen, and rarely spend time resting on blossoms. Seasonal timing is another clue. Females are present throughout the colony’s life cycle, but males become common mainly in late summer and fall, when new queens are emerging and mating takes place. INat susanna_h Hymenoptera (ants, bees, wasps, sawflies) are characterized by two pairs of membranous wings joined by tiny hooks (hamuli), chewing or chewing-sucking mouthparts, complete metamorphosis, and mandibulate mouthparts. Hymenoptera are predators. Hymenoptera order is split into sawflies (broad waist) and wasps/bees/ants (narrow waist). Key Characteristics of Hymenoptera: • Diversity: Over 150,000 described species worldwide, including ants, bees, wasps, and sawflies. • Wings: Typically two pairs of membranous wings; forewings larger than hindwings. The wings are coupled by hamuli (small hooks). Some castes (e.g., worker ants) are wingless. • Body Form:• In Symphyta (sawflies, horntails): broad connection between thorax and abdomen. • In Apocrita (ants, bees, wasps): narrow “wasp waist” between thorax and abdomen. • Mouthparts: Primarily mandibulate (chewing); in bees, modified into a chewing-lapping apparatus for nectar. • Metamorphosis: Holometabolous (complete metamorphosis: egg → larva → pupa → adult). • Feeding:• Sawfly larvae are herbivorous. • Many wasps are predatory or parasitoid, laying eggs in or on other insects. • Bees are nectar and pollen feeders, crucial pollinators. • Ants are omnivorous, with diverse diets. • Sociality: Includes some of the most advanced eusocial insects (ants, honeybees, some wasps), with division of labor, cooperative brood care, and overlapping generations. Most species, however, are solitary. • Ecological Role:• Pollinators (bees, some wasps). • Biological control agents (parasitoid wasps regulating pest populations). • Soil engineers and ecosystem influencers (ants). Yellow-faced Bumble Bees are large – ½ to ¾ inch (1.5 to 2 cm.) long - and their bodies and wings are mostly black. They have a fuzzy yellow head, including a yellow ‘head pile’ on the thorax just behind the actual head (see above) and a single yellow stripe on lower abdomen (males have a partial second stripe). Bombus vosnesenskii lives from about San Diego throughout most of California(except the desert areas), a little into Nevada around Reno, through Oregon, Washington up into Osoyoos British Columbia. This bumblebee is largely as summer bee with most of the hive living from April to September and is the most common bumblebee of California.

A Yellow-faced Bumblebee (Bombus vosnesenskii) pollinating the flowers of some Coast Woolly Sunflower (Eriophyllum staechadifolium) at Greyhound Rock County Park. The off-white/pale yellow coloration of the hairs on its clypeus (face), anterior scutum (front part of its thorax), and fourth tergites (abdominal segment) is due to natural variation; normally, these hairs are brighter yellow in color. This was a fairly common species at this location. This set has three shots of the same individual bee, taken as it flitted from flower to flower, hunting for nectar. The second shot is probably the best shot of it, as it shows the faint off-white/pale yellow hairs that cover the bee's anterior scutum, head, and clypeus. It also shows that the rest of the bee's hairs are black, except for those on its 4th tergites, which are also the same of-white/pale yellow color. This distribution of yellow and black hairs is a distinctive field mark for this species, separating it from all of the other bumblebees of western North America.

Photo comparison on BugGuide https://bugguide.net/index.php?q=search&keys=Bombus+vosnesenskii https://bugguide.net/index.php?q=search&keys=Bombus+caliginosus Link to confirmed observation of Yellow-faced Bumble Bee showing the underside: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/222367270 Genus Bombus (Bumblebees) are our only native social bees. They are warm blooded allowing them to fly at cooler temperatures than most pollinators. Native Bees https://openspacetrust.org/blog/native-bees/ Pollen Basket: The pollen basket is located on the female bee’s hind legs and consists of hairs surrounding a concave receptacle. As the bee visits a flower, she grooms herself and brushes pollen sticking to her body toward her hind legs. She then packs the pollen into the pollen basket. To help keep the pollen together during flight, some nectar is mixed in. Hairs on the pollen basket hold it all in place. Amazing! Kaufman Field Guide to Insects of North America, Eaton and Kaufman, 2006, p. 344-345. How to identify if it’s a Male or Female Bumble Bee: Male has no stinger so it can be handled if necessary. (per INat makarii_loskutov who handles many) “Generally, male bumblebees have hairy hind legs without a pollen basket (though beware female cuckoo bees, which also have hairy hind legs). Males also usually have more facial hair than females (either queens or workers) – and in several species this is a bright, obvious yellow. Males also generally have longer, more straggly hair, so if your bee has hairy legs, a moustache, and looks slightly unkempt it’s probably a male. Behavior can be a useful tool to separate males from workers and queens: because males do not have to collect pollen for the nest, they tend to sit lazily on flowers. They may also be observed flying along hedgerows searching for a mate. They do not feed during this time, so will land briefly on a surface, and then fly off again. They often patrol the same area for a while, so you may see the same bee repeating the circuit over and over again. In contrast, females tend to be much busier, flying quickly from flower to flower, and rarely wasting time by resting on flowers. The time of year can also be helpful – males become common in late summer and autumn, whereas females are present throughout the whole lifecycle." Bumble Bee I.D. Tips: https://www.bumblebeeconservation.org/identification-tips/ xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx "There are 6 taxonomic families of Bees: Apidae; (ap-ih-dee) These are the really common, really big bees. Included in this family are the European honeybees, BUMBLE BEES and carpenter bees. Andrenidae; (an-dren-ih-dee) These bees tend towards being small and hairy. They make their homes in the ground so are often called mining bees, or sand bees. Generally, they are so small they can fit in tiny flowers, like the bell-shaped blossoms that hang from Manzanita (Arctostaphylos). Colletidae; (co-lect-ih-dee) Included in this family are two genera (Colletes and Hylaeus) that are identifiable by their unique faces. If you are lucky enough to study the face of a landed Colletes, you can identify it by its distinctly triangular face. Hylaeus usually has a black body that is contrasted to the yellow markings on its face that make it look like it’s wearing a mask. Halictidae; (ha-lect-ih-dee) These bees are commonly called sweat bees because apparently, they like to land on human skin and drink sweat, although I’ve never observed this. I like to call them jewel bees because they often are metallic in sheen and bright in color. Megachilidae; (mega-chill-ih-dee) These bees include the mason or the wool-carder bees. They make their homes inside hollowed out twigs or in tunnels made by other insects like beetles. The invasive and common Anthidium manicatum is a regular visitor to the Santa Cruz mountains. Melittidae; (mel-it-tih-dee) The most-rare of the bee family types in California. Feeding exclusively on Clarkia flowers in the California chaparral, Hesperapis regularis is one of a small number of native species" Native Bees: Get to Know Native Bees of the Santa Cruz Mountains (California) with Obi Kaufmann. https://openspacetrust.org/blog/native-bees/

COMPARE Fog-belt Bumble Bee (Bombus caliginosus) Yellow abdominal stripes DO continue around underside. xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx COMPARE TO Yellow-faced Bumble Bee (Bombus vosnesenskii) is in the Honey Bees, Bumble Bees, and Allies (Apidae) family. It is about 16mm long. Yellow abdominal stripe DOES NOT continue around underside in this species. "There is a very similar species, Bombus caliginosus, that has a range that overlaps with Yellow-faced Bumble Bee (B. vosnesenskii). The easiest way to tell the two apart is to look at the yellow abdominal stripe. In B. caliginosus, it continues on the underside, while in B. vosnesenskii, the underside is black." Per INat @ domingozungri. Photo comparison on BugGuide https://bugguide.net/index.php?q=search&keys=Bombus+vosnesenskii https://bugguide.net/index.php?q=search&keys=Bombus+caliginosus Link to confirmed observation of Yellow-faced Bumble Bee showing the underside: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/222367270 And a few more: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?taxon_id=57689&user_id=aparrot1&verifiable=any Genus Bombus (Bumblebees) are our only native social bees. They are warm blooded allowing them to fly at cooler temperatures than most pollinators. Native Bees https://openspacetrust.org/blog/native-bees/ Pollen Basket: The pollen basket is located on the female bee’s hind legs and consists of hairs surrounding a concave receptacle. As the bee visits a flower, she grooms herself and brushes pollen sticking to her body toward her hind legs. She then packs the pollen into the pollen basket. To help keep the pollen together during flight, some nectar is mixed in. Hairs on the pollen basket hold it all in place. Amazing! Kaufman Field Guide to Insects of North America, Eaton and Kaufman, 2006, p. 344-345. How to identify if it’s a Male or Female Bumble Bee: Male has no stinger so it can be handled if necessary. (per INat makarii_loskutov who handles many) “Generally, male bumblebees have hairy hind legs without a pollen basket (though beware female cuckoo bees, which also have hairy hind legs). Males also usually have more facial hair than females (either queens or workers) – and in several species this is a bright, obvious yellow. Males also generally have longer, more straggly hair, so if your bee has hairy legs, a moustache, and looks slightly unkempt it’s probably a male. Behavior can be a useful tool to separate males from workers and queens: because males do not have to collect pollen for the nest, they tend to sit lazily on flowers. They may also be observed flying along hedgerows searching for a mate. They do not feed during this time, so will land briefly on a surface, and then fly off again. They often patrol the same area for a while, so you may see the same bee repeating the circuit over and over again. In contrast, females tend to be much busier, flying quickly from flower to flower, and rarely wasting time by resting on flowers. The time of year can also be helpful – males become common in late summer and autumn, whereas females are present throughout the whole lifecycle." xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx Irene's Bumble Bees (Bombus genus) on INaturalist, worldwide: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?taxon_id=52775&user_id=aparrot1&verifiable=any Irene's Bees (Epifamily Anthophila) on INaturalist, worldwide: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?taxon_id=630955&user_id=aparrot1 Bees (Epifamily Anthophila) "Bees forage on nectar and pollen--nectar as an energy source and pollen for protein and other nutrients. Bee pollination is important both ecologically and commercially. Bees provide crucial ecological services that enhance ecosystem resilience, food security and support the agricultural economy. There has been a huge decline of bees worldwide in the past few decades, primarily due to human pesticide use to kill other insects, and habitat loss of native plants. Included in this family are the European honeybees, Bumble Bees and Carpenter Bees. Andrenidae; (an-dren-ih-dee) These bees tend towards being small and hairy. They make their homes in the ground so are often called mining bees, or sand bees. Generally, they are so small they can fit in tiny flowers, like the bell-shaped blossoms that hang from Manzanita (Arctostaphylos). Colletidae; (co-lect-ih-dee) Included in this family are two genera (Colletes and Hylaeus) that are identifiable by their unique faces. If you are lucky enough to study the face of a landed Colletes, you can identify it by its distinctly triangular face. Hylaeus usually has a black body that is contrasted to the yellow markings on its face that make it look like it’s wearing a mask. Halictidae; (ha-lect-ih-dee) These bees are commonly called sweat bees because apparently, they like to land on human skin and drink sweat, although I’ve never observed this. I like to call them jewel bees because they often are metallic in sheen and bright in color. Megachilidae; (mega-chill-ih-dee) These bees include the mason or the wool-carder bees. They make their homes inside hollowed out twigs or in tunnels made by other insects like beetles. The invasive and common Anthidium manicatum is a regular visitor to the Santa Cruz mountains. Melittidae; (mel-it-tih-dee) The most-rare of the bee family types in California. I spotted this Yellow-faced Bumblebee (Bombus vosensenskii) working a large patch of Rose Clover (Trifolium hirtum) at Russian Ridge Open Space Preserve, and I found myself following it and attempting to take its picture. The shots that came out reasonably well remind me of "Where's Waldo" pictures, with the bee playing the part of Waldo. The best of these shots is the lead photo. Here, the Yellow-faced Bumblebee came close enough for me to take a reasonably decent close-up photo of it, one that fortuitously shows the diagnostic yellow patch on its face. The California Bumblebee (Bombus californicus) is very similar in size and appearance, but lacks this yellow facial patch. The lead photo also shows the yellow band on its thorax, its eyes (one on either side of the yellow face patch), its antenna (emerging from the yellow face patch), and - if you look carefully - a bit of its tongue, which it is inserting into the corolla tube of an individual clover flower for a sip of nectar. They are warm blooded allowing them to fly at cooler temperatures than most pollinators. Native Bees https://openspacetrust.org/blog/native-bees/ Pollen Basket: The pollen basket is located on the female bee’s hind legs and consists of hairs surrounding a concave receptacle. As the bee visits a flower, she grooms herself and brushes pollen sticking to her body toward her hind legs. She then packs the pollen into the pollen basket. To help keep the pollen together during flight, some nectar is mixed in. Hairs on the pollen basket hold it all in place. Amazing! Kaufman Field Guide to Insects of North America, Eaton and Kaufman, 2006, p. 344-345. How to identify if it’s a Male or Female Bumble Bee: Male has no stinger so it can be handled if necessary. (per INat makarii_loskutov who handles many) “Generally, male bumblebees have hairy hind legs without a pollen basket (though beware female cuckoo bees, which also have hairy hind legs). Males also usually have more facial hair than females (either queens or workers) – and in several species this is a bright, obvious yellow. Males also generally have longer, more straggly hair, so if your bee has hairy legs, a moustache, and looks slightly unkempt it’s probably a male. Behavior can be a useful tool to separate males from workers and queens: because males do not have to collect pollen for the nest, they tend to sit lazily on flowers. They may also be observed flying along hedgerows searching for a mate. They do not feed during this time, so will land briefly on a surface, and then fly off again. They often patrol the same area for a while, so you may see the same bee repeating the circuit over and over again. In contrast, females tend to be much busier, flying quickly from flower to flower, and rarely wasting time by resting on flowers. The time of year can also be helpful – males become common in late summer and autumn, whereas females are present throughout the whole lifecycle." Bumble Bee I.D. Tips: https://www.bumblebeeconservation.org/identification-tips/ xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx "There are 6 taxonomic families of Bees: Apidae; (ap-ih-dee) These are the really common, really big bees. Included in this family are the European honeybees, BUMBLE BEES and carpenter bees. Andrenidae; (an-dren-ih-dee) These bees tend towards being small and hairy. They make their homes in the ground so are often called mining bees, or sand bees. Generally, they are so small they can fit in tiny flowers, like the bell-shaped blossoms that hang from Manzanita (Arctostaphylos). Colletidae; (co-lect-ih-dee) Included in this family are two genera (Colletes and Hylaeus) that are identifiable by their unique faces. If you are lucky enough to study the face of a landed Colletes, you can identify it by its distinctly triangular face. Hylaeus usually has a black body that is contrasted to the yellow markings on its face that make it look like it’s wearing a mask. Halictidae; (ha-lect-ih-dee) These bees are commonly called sweat bees because apparently, they like to land on human skin and drink sweat, although I’ve never observed this. I like to call them jewel bees because they often are metallic in sheen and bright in color. Megachilidae; (mega-chill-ih-dee) These bees include the mason or the wool-carder bees. They make their homes inside hollowed out twigs or in tunnels made by other insects like beetles. The invasive and common Anthidium manicatum is a regular visitor to the Santa Cruz mountains. Melittidae; (mel-it-tih-dee) The most-rare of the bee family types in California. Feeding exclusively on Clarkia flowers in the California chaparral, Hesperapis regularis is one of a small number of native species" Native Bees: Get to Know Native Bees of the Santa Cruz Mountains (California) with Obi Kaufmann. https://openspacetrust.org/blog/native-bees/

COMPARE Fog-belt Bumble Bee (Bombus caliginosus) Yellow abdominal stripes DO continue around underside. xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx COMPARE TO Yellow-faced Bumble Bee (Bombus vosnesenskii) is in the Honey Bees, Bumble Bees, and Allies (Apidae) family. It is about 16mm long. Yellow abdominal stripe DOES NOT continue around underside in this species. "There is a very similar species, Bombus caliginosus, that has a range that overlaps with Yellow-faced Bumble Bee (B. vosnesenskii). The easiest way to tell the two apart is to look at the yellow abdominal stripe. In B. caliginosus, it continues on the underside, while in B. vosnesenskii, the underside is black." Per INat @ domingozungri. Photo comparison on BugGuide https://bugguide.net/index.php?q=search&keys=Bombus+vosnesenskii https://bugguide.net/index.php?q=search&keys=Bombus+caliginosus Link to confirmed observation of Yellow-faced Bumble Bee showing the underside: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/222367270 And a few more: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?taxon_id=57689&user_id=aparrot1&verifiable=any Genus Bombus (Bumblebees) are our only native social bees. They are warm blooded allowing them to fly at cooler temperatures than most pollinators. Native Bees https://openspacetrust.org/blog/native-bees/ Pollen Basket: The pollen basket is located on the female bee’s hind legs and consists of hairs surrounding a concave receptacle. As the bee visits a flower, she grooms herself and brushes pollen sticking to her body toward her hind legs. She then packs the pollen into the pollen basket. To help keep the pollen together during flight, some nectar is mixed in. Hairs on the pollen basket hold it all in place. Amazing! Kaufman Field Guide to Insects of North America, Eaton and Kaufman, 2006, p. 344-345. How to identify if it’s a Male or Female Bumble Bee: Male has no stinger so it can be handled if necessary. (per INat makarii_loskutov who handles many) “Generally, male bumblebees have hairy hind legs without a pollen basket (though beware female cuckoo bees, which also have hairy hind legs). Males also usually have more facial hair than females (either queens or workers) – and in several species this is a bright, obvious yellow. Males also generally have longer, more straggly hair, so if your bee has hairy legs, a moustache, and looks slightly unkempt it’s probably a male. Behavior can be a useful tool to separate males from workers and queens: because males do not have to collect pollen for the nest, they tend to sit lazily on flowers. They may also be observed flying along hedgerows searching for a mate. They do not feed during this time, so will land briefly on a surface, and then fly off again. They often patrol the same area for a while, so you may see the same bee repeating the circuit over and over again. In contrast, females tend to be much busier, flying quickly from flower to flower, and rarely wasting time by resting on flowers. The time of year can also be helpful – males become common in late summer and autumn, whereas females are present throughout the whole lifecycle." xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx Irene's Bumble Bees (Bombus genus) on INaturalist, worldwide: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?taxon_id=52775&user_id=aparrot1&verifiable=any Irene's Bees (Epifamily Anthophila) on INaturalist, worldwide: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?taxon_id=630955&user_id=aparrot1 Bees (Epifamily Anthophila) "Bees forage on nectar and pollen--nectar as an energy source and pollen for protein and other nutrients. Most pollen is used as food for bee larvae. Predators of bees include birds such as bee-eaters, insect predators such as dragonflies, and mammals. Bee pollination is important both ecologically and commercially. Bees provide crucial ecological services that enhance ecosystem resilience, food security and support the agricultural economy. There has been a huge decline of bees worldwide in the past few decades, primarily due to human pesticide use to kill other insects, and habitat loss of native plants. "There are 6 Taxonomic Families of Bees (Epifamily Anthophila): https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/630955-Anthophila: Miner, Fairy, Allied Panurgine, and Oxaeine Bees (Family Andrenidae) Honey Bees, Bumble Bees, and Allies (Family Apidae) Plasterer Bees (Family Colletidae) Sweat Bees (Family Halictidae) Mason, Leafcutter, Carder, and Resin Bees (Family Megachilidae) Melittid Bees (Family Melittidae) Swift and Comb-bearer Bees (Family Stenotritidae) Beekeeping Beyond the Hive: The Surprising Secrets of Bees Native • Wild • Managed "Bees are the wispy sprites that connect the plant kingdom to the animal kingdom; they are the ties that bind the natural world together. Powell, 2nd ed., 2020 BugGuide: Arthropods: Photos of Insects, Spiders & Their Kin (US & Canada): https://bugguide.net/node/view/3/bgpage Native Bees: Get to Know Native Bees of the Santa Cruz Mountains (California) with Obi Kaufmann: https://openspacetrust.org/blog/native-bees/ Apidae; (ap-ih-dee) These are the really common, really big bees. Included in this family are the European honeybees, Bumble Bees and Carpenter Bees. Andrenidae; (an-dren-ih-dee) These bees tend towards being small and hairy. They make their homes in the ground so are often called mining bees, or sand bees. Generally, they are so small they can fit in tiny flowers, like the bell-shaped blossoms that hang from Manzanita (Arctostaphylos). Colletidae; (co-lect-ih-dee) Included in this family are two genera (Colletes and Hylaeus) that are identifiable by their unique faces. If you are lucky enough to study the face of a landed Colletes, you can identify it by its distinctly triangular face. Hylaeus usually has a black body that is contrasted to the yellow markings on its face that make it look like it’s wearing a mask. Halictidae; (ha-lect-ih-dee) These bees are commonly called sweat bees because apparently, they like to land on human skin and drink sweat, although I’ve never observed this. I like to call them jewel bees because they often are metallic in sheen and bright in color. Megachilidae; (mega-chill-ih-dee) These bees include the mason or the wool-carder bees. They make their homes inside hollowed out twigs or in tunnels made by other insects like beetles. The invasive and common Anthidium manicatum is a regular visitor to the Santa Cruz mountains. Melittidae; (mel-it-tih-dee) The most-rare of the bee family types in California. Feeding exclusively on Clarkia flowers in the California chaparral, Hesperapis regularis is one of a small number of native species" Native Bees: Get to Know Native Bees of the Santa Cruz Mountains with Obi Kaufmann. Native Bees https://openspacetrust.org/blog/native-bees/ Pollen Basket: The pollen basket is located on the female bee’s hind legs and consists of hairs surrounding a concave receptacle. As the bee visits a flower, she grooms herself and brushes pollen sticking to her body toward her hind legs. She then packs the pollen into the pollen basket. Kaufman Field Guide to Insects of North America, Eaton and Kaufman, 2006, p. 344-345. How to identify if it’s a Male or Female Bumble Bee: Male has no stinger so it can be handled if necessary. (per INat makarii_loskutov who handles many) “Generally, male bumblebees have hairy hind legs without a pollen basket (though beware female cuckoo bees, which also have hairy hind legs). Males also usually have more facial hair than females (either queens or workers) – and in several species this is a bright, obvious yellow. Males also generally have longer, more straggly hair, so if your bee has hairy legs, a moustache, and looks slightly unkempt it’s probably a male. Behavior can be a useful tool to separate males from workers and queens: because males do not have to collect pollen for the nest, they tend to sit lazily on flowers. They may also be observed flying along hedgerows searching for a mate. They do not feed during this time, so will land briefly on a surface, and then fly off again. They often patrol the same area for a while, so you may see the same bee repeating the circuit over and over again. In contrast, females tend to be much busier, flying quickly from flower to flower, and rarely wasting time by resting on flowers. The time of year can also be helpful – males become common in late summer and autumn, whereas females are present throughout the whole lifecycle." Bumble Bee I.D. Tips: https://www.bumblebeeconservation.org/identification-tips/ xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx "There are 6 taxonomic families of Bees: Apidae; (ap-ih-dee) These are the really common, really big bees. Included in this family are the European honeybees, BUMBLE BEES and carpenter bees. Andrenidae; (an-dren-ih-dee) These bees tend towards being small and hairy. They make their homes in the ground so are often called mining bees, or sand bees. Generally, they are so small they can fit in tiny flowers, like the bell-shaped blossoms that hang from Manzanita (Arctostaphylos). Colletidae; (co-lect-ih-dee) Included in this family are two genera (Colletes and Hylaeus) that are identifiable by their unique faces. If you are lucky enough to study the face of a landed Colletes, you can identify it by its distinctly triangular face. Hylaeus usually has a black body that is contrasted to the yellow markings on its face that make it look like it’s wearing a mask. Halictidae; (ha-lect-ih-dee) These bees are commonly called sweat bees because apparently, they like to land on human skin and drink sweat, although I’ve never observed this. I like to call them jewel bees because they often are metallic in sheen and bright in color. Megachilidae; (mega-chill-ih-dee) These bees include the mason or the wool-carder bees. They make their homes inside hollowed out twigs or in tunnels made by other insects like beetles. The invasive and common Anthidium manicatum is a regular visitor to the Santa Cruz mountains. Melittidae; (mel-it-tih-dee) The most-rare of the bee family types in California. Feeding exclusively on Clarkia flowers in the California chaparral, Hesperapis regularis is one of a small number of native species" Native Bees: Get to Know Native Bees of the Santa Cruz Mountains (California) with Obi Kaufmann. https://openspacetrust.org/blog/native-bees/

The simplest difference is that males do not have a stinger, so they cannot sting. Their hind legs are also a good clue: males have hairy hind legs without a pollen basket, while females (workers and queens) have a smooth, shiny area on the hind leg used for carrying pollen. One caution is that female cuckoo bumble bees also lack pollen baskets, so leg hair alone is not always enough. Males usually have more facial hair than females, and in some species this hair is bright yellow and easy to see. Their overall hair tends to be longer and messier, giving them a slightly unkempt look compared with the neater appearance of workers and queens. Behavior also helps. Because males do not collect pollen for a nest, they often sit on flowers for long periods or rest between short flights. They may patrol along hedges, forest edges, or trails while searching for females, flying a repeated route and landing briefly before taking off again. Females behave differently: they move quickly from flower to flower, gather pollen, and rarely spend time resting on blossoms. Seasonal timing is another clue. Females are present throughout the colony’s life cycle, but males become common mainly in late summer and fall, when new queens are emerging and mating takes place. INat susanna_h Hymenoptera (ants, bees, wasps, sawflies) are characterized by two pairs of membranous wings joined by tiny hooks (hamuli), chewing or chewing-sucking mouthparts, complete metamorphosis, and mandibulate mouthparts. Hymenoptera are predators. Hymenoptera order is split into sawflies (broad waist) and wasps/bees/ants (narrow waist). Key Characteristics of Hymenoptera: • Diversity: Over 150,000 described species worldwide, including ants, bees, wasps, and sawflies. • Wings: Typically two pairs of membranous wings; forewings larger than hindwings. The wings are coupled by hamuli (small hooks). Some castes (e.g., worker ants) are wingless. • Body Form:• In Symphyta (sawflies, horntails): broad connection between thorax and abdomen. • In Apocrita (ants, bees, wasps): narrow “wasp waist” between thorax and abdomen. • Mouthparts: Primarily mandibulate (chewing); in bees, modified into a chewing-lapping apparatus for nectar. • Metamorphosis: Holometabolous (complete metamorphosis: egg → larva → pupa → adult). • Feeding:• Sawfly larvae are herbivorous. • Many wasps are predatory or parasitoid, laying eggs in or on other insects. • Bees are nectar and pollen feeders, crucial pollinators. • Ants are omnivorous, with diverse diets. • Sociality: Includes some of the most advanced eusocial insects (ants, honeybees, some wasps), with division of labor, cooperative brood care, and overlapping generations. Most species, however, are solitary. • Ecological Role:• Pollinators (bees, some wasps). • Biological control agents (parasitoid wasps regulating pest populations). • Soil engineers and ecosystem influencers (ants). Yellow-faced Bumble Bees are large – ½ to ¾ inch (1.5 to 2 cm.) long - and their bodies and wings are mostly black. They have a fuzzy yellow head, including a yellow ‘head pile’ on the thorax just behind the actual head (see above) and a single yellow stripe on lower abdomen (males have a partial second stripe). Bombus vosnesenskii lives from about San Diego throughout most of California(except the desert areas), a little into Nevada around Reno, through Oregon, Washington up into Osoyoos British Columbia. This bumblebee is largely as summer bee with most of the hive living from April to September and is the most common bumblebee of California.
